en: The Mysterious Pivot of Contemplating the Mind, Volume One:
"To accord with reality is to be near it; it does not reside in physical proximity. When those of merit appear in the world, precious jewels manifest; when those of meager merit appear, thorns grow.
All this arises from one's own mind, whether [the truth] manifests or does not manifest. As in the verse of the maiden Candrottarā in response to Śāriputra:
Lizi said: "Though I was within my inner chamber, the Venerable One appeared as if before my very eyes. You, O benevolent one, are called an Arhat;

though you are always with me, you do not see me. Thus, Subhūti did not leave his stone chamber yet personally beheld the Dharma-body, while Ānanda, though serving as the Buddha’s attendant, did not see the Buddha’s face."

If one does not contemplate the mind, how can one be liberated from the bonds of objects? This is because one does not know that what arises as a transformation of one's own consciousness is then taken as an object by oneself.

It is like a painter who creates various forms and, in turn, develops attachment to them; with the brush of the mental consciousness, he sketches the map of the three realms, and as soon as distinctions of high and low are made, love and hate arise accordingly.
It is also like a spring silkworm spinning its cocoon or an autumn moth flying into a lamp—bound by one's own evil views.
Ignorance consumes itself. This method of contemplating the mind can be known through direct experience. Just as in a night dream there is only mind, so it is upon awakening.
Furthermore, that which sees within a dream is the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) of the dream state; that which sees in the present is the clear and distinct mental consciousness.

Objects of the past and future are perceived by the solitary, distracted mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*). Those seen within meditative concentration (*samādhi*) are perceived by the mental consciousness within concentration.
Thus, whether dreaming or waking, whether distracted or in concentration, all do not transcend these four types of mental consciousness.

For instance, when one presently perceives an object such as something blue or white, within that direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), one apprehends the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of the phenomenon without being accompanied by names and words, and without a mind of deliberation.
This is the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*). One does not grasp it as external form;

rather, it is entirely the seeing-portion (*darśana-bhāga*) of the visual consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*), which, together with the simultaneously arising clear mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), uses inference (*anumāna*) to conceptually discriminate and judge it as "blue," thereby forming an external interpretation.

Because the mind discriminates it as "form" and verbalizes it as "blue," it is said that these are all conceptual discriminations of mental discourse (*manojalpa-vikalpa*). This is like the visual consciousness acting spontaneously and impulsively.
At the moment of seeing, before black and white have been distinguished, one flows into the mental ground (*manobhūmi*) in an instant, whereupon it is grasped and formed into an object.

When the mind takes this as its condition, visual consciousness has already passed away. Yet most people in the world stubbornly cling to the notion, "I see with my own eyes," which is entirely devoid of reason.
To fail to return to the luminous essence of the nature of seeing within oneself, but instead to seek it externally and learn from others through delusion, is like drilling water in search of fire.
To press sand to extract oil is not the correct cause; it is merely a waste of effort.

If one can discipline oneself to resolve matters and clearly realize one's own mind, it will be like producing fire from wood or extracting oil from sesame seeds—without violating the correct cause, accomplishment is easily attained.

Without being separated by even a single thought-moment, the power [of practice] is established instantaneously. Thus, firm faith remains unshakable; the empty echoes of the "emptiness of dharmas" naturally subside.
Its clarity and sincerity can be verified: the wild flames of the spirit-dampened field suddenly cease. There is no need for external mediation; the mental demons are abruptly severed.

It does not rely on other techniques; consciousness suddenly dissolves. Unless one removes the unwholesome person, this principle cannot be fathomed. Therefore it is said: "relying on wisdom and not on consciousness.
This means that consciousness is in active operation, making discriminations according to sensory objects—eyes and forms, ears and sounds—and thus remains mired in delusion without awakening.
The Great Sage taught that objects are one's own mind; yet the ignorant and dull-witted cling to them as if they were external to consciousness.

Today, people recite the doctrine of emptiness with their mouths, yet their minds have not yet abandoned the notion of existence. They cannot rise into the air, and it is even more difficult for them to enter fire. This is because they are all bound by delusion regarding the manifestations of the mind.
Once they attain penetration, these manifestations function according to the mind; would this not be like a bird soaring through the sky, which naturally leaves no trace upon the cloth?

It is not surprising that [the robe] was washed in fire. However, because the cognitive natures (*vijñāna*) of sentient beings differ, the Great Sage has provided distinct teachings according to their dispositions.
Yet, based on the ultimate Way (*paramārtha*), it is simply one's own mind; thus it is said: "The phenomena of the three realms, from the highest to the lowest, are in truth nothing but mind."
This explains the mind by way of the world as the dependent retribution (*pariṇāma-vipāka*). Furthermore, it says:

"Suchness (*tathatā*), the reality-limit (*bhūtakoṭi*), nirvāṇa, and the various types of mind-made bodies (*manomaya-kāya*) within the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*)—I declare these to be the measure of the mind (*cittamātra*). This explains the mind by way of the supramundane essence of phenomena.
Ultimately reaching the reality, one arrives completely at this source. According to one's inclinations, fruits are experienced; yet returning to the fundamental, one realizes the definitive meaning.
Furthermore, all objective realms are merely the deluded movement of the mind; if the mind does not arise, all appearances of objective realms cease, leaving only the single true mind.

Pervading all places, and further relying on the fact that the objects of consciousness-only have no intrinsic substance from the beginning: since the object does not arise, the mind also follows in cessation.
Because the mind is the support (*āśraya*) and the object is that which depends upon it (*āśrita*), once the support has ceased, that which depends upon it does not arise.
Thus, doubt dissolves along with subject and object; the vine and the snake are simultaneously emptied. Seeing ceases as its antidote, and form and name are thereby both stilled.
If one does not contemplate the mind, how can one cease conceptualization? For all conceptualizations are merely conceptualizations of one's own mind;
the mind does not perceive the mind, and no characteristic can be apprehended. As a verse says: "Phenomena arise from conceptualization, and they likewise cease through conceptualization."

One extinguishes these various conceptual constructions. This Dharma is neither arising nor ceasing; arising and ceasing are merely the mind. The Dharma is without movement or stillness. Furthermore, as a verse says: "Various things revolve according to the mind;
it is mind alone, not other dharmas. When the mind arises, all variety arises; when the mind ceases, all variety ceases.
Sentient beings engage in false conceptualization, seeing objects where there are no objects. There is no external referent—there is only mind; there is no conceptual construction."
One attains liberation. Why is liberation attained? Because one realizes that there is only mind (*cittamātra*).

It is like the sixth consciousness, which arises independently and in a distracted state, taking as its objects the past and future, water-moons, mirror-images, and so forth; these transform and give rise to false objective parts (*nimitta-bhāga*).

These objective parts are merely the false conceptualizations and mental constructions of the sixth consciousness of sentient beings, arising in accordance with their own perceptions; they do not exist at all as real objects external to the mind.
Thus one knows that by entering this gate of contemplation, one thoroughly penetrates all phenomena; it is like an arrow shot at the ground—there is nowhere it does not hit.
If one does not enter into this principle, one will merely follow after others; it is like an arrow shot at a target—mostly missing and rarely hitting. As a verse says:
"Acting within one's own domain, one obtains what ought to be obtained; Acting within the domain of another, one is like a fish fallen onto dry land."
If one does not contemplate the mind, what consciousness could perceive illusion? By grasping one's own mind with one's own mind, that which is not illusory becomes an illusory phenomenon.

If there is no grasping, there is nothing that is not illusory; since that which is non-illusory never arises, from where could illusory phenomena be established? Furthermore, it is said: "All things are like illusions."

That illusion is unreal; one knows that illusion is illusion. By guarding the truth and embracing the One, once one realizes that all things are empty, one immediately returns to the Oneness of the True Mind.
Furthermore, it is said: "Wholesome and unwholesome dharmas are produced through transformation from the mind. All objective realms are conceptualizations of mental discourse.
By restraining them in a single place, all conditions are severed and extinguished. Thus, one knows that receiving bodies within the six destinies is solely a transformation of what is conjured.
The phenomena within the three realms are all produced by mental fabrication.

They are no different from treading upon a city in the sky (*gandharvanagara*), thirsting for water in a mirage, hoping for the fruiting of flowers in the air, or expecting a woman carved from stone to give birth to a child. Like a courtesan appearing on a stage, they delude the eye of wisdom;
like a magician wandering through a gathering, they merely deceive one's own mind. Constantly immersed in such delusion, who is able to observe them clearly? One must know this with certainty.
There is no other principle; it arises solely from the deluded mind. It serves as the root-stump for the eight inversions and the source-cavity for the four torrents.
It is as swift as a flash of lightning and as violent as a raging wind. It stirs up worldly toil like a sudden gust, and its rapidity exceeds that of a cascading river.
Greed and desire suddenly arise, more urgent than a whirling wheel of fire. Thus, one constructs the four Māras, drives the ten afflictions, and sinks into the two [extremes].

They sink to the bottom of the river of death and cast themselves into the flames of the eight sufferings. Intoxicated and deluded, they fail to find the pearl within their robes; they undergo hardships in vain.
They struggle to lose the jewel in their foreheads, crying out in grief for nothing. All this is due to the deluded mind, which is confused by this true awakening.

Know, therefore, that rising or falling depends on oneself; loss or gain is not caused by another. What is falsely created and falsely cultivated must be experienced by oneself alone; there are certainly no external objects.
Thus one applies the remedy. For example, in the past there was a bhikṣu who, at night, mistakenly stepped on a melon rind, thinking it to be a frog;
because of this, he suffered in the evil realms. Therefore, when goodness arises from the mind, it blesses one's own person, just as a jewel manifests light that in turn illuminates the jewel itself.
When evil arises from the mind, it conversely harms oneself, just as rust produced by iron corrodes and destroys its very form. Thus...

The gentleman values turning back upon himself; he does not resent Heaven nor blame others. How much more so for one who aspires to the Way and participates in the Mystery—how could such a person fail to believe this principle?

If one does not contemplate the mind, how can one practice giving? When there is nothing with which to give, it is called *dāna* (giving). If there were dharmas outside the mind, there would be something to be given;
the subject and object would not vanish, and one would fail to realize that the three wheels are empty in essence. This is because one must enter the dharma-realm of giving.

If one does not contemplate the mind, how can one maintain the precepts? According to the Mahāyāna Bodhisattva Precepts, one contemplates that there is only mind; fundamentally, there are no external forms.
Since there are no forms to be violated, even the characteristics of emptiness do not exist. Because one is free from the fault of grasping at signs, it is called "maintaining the precepts.

It is further said: "The precepts of all ordinary beings and sages take the mind as their essence. Therefore, it is said: "Though one may believe in distinct characteristics, one does not believe in a single essence."

Because they lack the characteristic of non-differentiation, they are said to be incomplete in faith; consequently, their observance of the precepts is also incomplete, and their extensive learning is likewise incomplete.
If one does not contemplate the mind, how can there be patience? Therefore it is said: "Patience, in a single kṣaṇa, exhausts all marks (*lakṣaṇa*) and all objects of perception (*ālambana*).
One knows that this is "mind-only" (*cittamātra*), and that there is no external object to be countered; only then is it called patience. Thus it is said:
if the object of insult were like a tortoise's hair, only then would true patience be realized.
If one does not contemplate the mind, how can one achieve diligence? Therefore it is said: "If the mind does not arise, diligence will be boundless.
Thus we know that as soon as the mind arises, there is an objective sphere to be perceived; only when one realizes that both mind and object are empty does one truly achieve diligence.
If one does not contemplate the mind, how can meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) be accomplished? Therefore, if one does not differentiate among various objects, this is the true taming of the mind.

To realize that all phenomena are empty is to be constantly in *samādhi*. Thus it is said: "The meditative concentration of a Great Bodhisattva refers to contemplating that there is only consciousness (*vijñaptimātra*);
when no object is perceived, the mind is free from discursive thought, which is true emptiness. As a verse says: "Human life..."
Even a hundred years of life spent in much indulgence and negligence is not equal to a single day of turning the mind toward emptiness and stillness.
If one does not contemplate the mind, how can *prajñā* be realized? It is through the wisdom-nature of the spiritual palace that all Buddhas are born;
it is the guide upon perilous paths, the bright torch within a dark chamber of delusion, and the wise oar in the sea of birth and death. [The afflictions...]

It is the skilled physician for the affliction of suffering; the great wind that shatters the mountain of heterodoxy; the valiant general who destroys the armies of Māra; the blazing sun that illuminates the dark paths;
the sudden thunder that awakens昏沉 (dull) consciousness; the golden probe that extracts the cataracts of ignorance and blindness;

the nectar that quenches the thirst of craving; the sharp blade of wisdom that severs the ribs of delusion; and the precious jewel that provides relief to the poor. If Prajñā were not clear, ten thousand...
Thus, practice becomes a mere empty pretension. Hence it is said: "If one does not recognize the profound principle, one’s efforts at contemplating purity are in vain. It is further stated:

"Not seeking the nature, characteristics, causes, or conditions of all phenomena is called right wisdom. This refers to the fact that when the nature of the mind is unborn, one can achieve wondrous wisdom.

Therefore, the great Bodhisattvas of wisdom all contemplate their own minds; they take the conceptualizations of mental discourse as their objective realm from the very moment they first resolve to attain enlightenment.

From the initial stage of the mind until the attainment of Buddhahood, one should always perform this contemplation. Because it is merely the discrimination of the mind of consciousness-only, one perceives that no external objects exist;
ultimately, there is only the single true emptiness, and nothing else whatsoever. Therefore, it is said: "The empty mind is unmoving, and it fully possesses the six pāramitās."
If one does not contemplate the mind, how can skillful means be established? The Bodhisattva takes non-attainment as skillful means and is thus able to enter the boundless net of illusions;
because they gather sentient beings through the four methods of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*), there is no phenomenon apart from the mind—what, then, could be attained?

If one does not contemplate the mind, how can great vows be accomplished? Since vows arise from the mind, they are called an ocean of vows. The world that is sustained depends solely upon the wind-circle;
the myriad practices that are bestowed depend solely upon the ocean of vows.
If one does not contemplate the mind, how can power be achieved? Therefore it is said: "If the substance is subtle, the momentum is weighty; if the substance is heavy, the momentum is slight.
For example, because the substance of earth is heavy, its momentum is not equal to that of water. Because the nature of water is heavy, its force is not equal to that of fire.
Fire is not equal to wind, and wind is not equal to the mind. Because the mind is formless, its power is unsurpassed. Its supernormal powers and transformations are inconceivable in eight ways.
Deliberation is the power of the mind. This power can encompass all things and accomplish all things.

It is like a mother fish remembering her offspring, or a queen bee gathering her bees. If the mother fish does not remember them, her offspring will not be born; if the queen bee does not gather them, the swarm will not assemble.
All lands are sustained by the power of perception (*saṃjñā*); various objective conditions arrive in accordance with thought. Perception is empty.
Thus, when the object is stilled, thought ceases and signs vanish. As a verse says: "All phenomena are not solid; they depend solely upon the establishment of mindfulness.
For one who perceives emptiness through understanding, there is no conceptualization whatsoever."
If one does not contemplate the mind, how can wisdom be realized? Taking the mind as wisdom is precisely the function of the inherent nature’s quiescent illumination.
This wisdom is possessed by both ordinary beings and sages; it is only that its application varies in depth and shallowness. Thus it is said:

"Those who are perfectly enlightened all day long yet have never experienced perfect enlightenment are ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*); those who wish to realize perfect enlightenment yet have not reached its ultimate limit are Bodhisattvas. [This is] the sustaining power.
Perfect Enlightenment (Samantabhadra-bodhi). One who is fully endowed with Perfect Enlightenment is the Tathāgata. Apart from Perfect Enlightenment, there are no six realms of existence;

apart from Perfect Enlightenment, there are no Three Vehicles; without Perfect Enlightenment, there is no Tathāgata; and if Perfect Enlightenment were extinguished, there would be no True Dharma. In reality, all are but a single Way.
This is what the Buddhas of the three periods have realized; indeed, they have realized this. It is for this Great Matter that the Tathāgata has appeared in the world. Indeed...
It is for this purpose that the Three Piṭakas, the Twelve Divisions of the Canon, and all the Sūtras serve as expositions thereof.

These are teachings that exhaust the ultimate source and discourses that accord with the nature of reality (*dharmatā*). They are like the revelation of the Dharma-gate of the Universal Eye, wherein each describes but one aspect of the underlying principle;
they resemble the unrolling of the scrolls of the Great Trichiliocosm, wherein not a single word remains outside the mind. Thus, they encompass the entire net by extracting its very essence.
In a single word, nothing is left unexhausted. Thus, the provisional reveals the real; though the specific teachings differ, they are no other than one another.
Amidst the abundance of manifold meanings, it is like selecting jade from stone; within the multitude of scriptures, it is as if picking gold from sand. It illuminates the lamp of non-dual wisdom.
It shatters the dark delusions of the sensory dusts and pours forth the water of single-flavored wisdom. It washes away the false defilements of the mental ground.
If one can enter the divine through a single phrase, it shall serve as the seed for kalpas to come. Why is this? Because this dharma-gate of the mind, among all multitudes, [is supreme].
It is the leader and the teacher; it is the illumination and the Way. Therefore it is said: "Among all phenomena, the mind is the foremost.
Furthermore, "Among all illuminations, the illumination of the mind is supreme. Moreover, the Buddha takes the Dharma as his teacher, thus saying: "This matter is known only by me.
It is like a mirror hung upon a high terrace, or like an eye suspended in the vast expanse of space. When the solitary light shines once, all myriad concerns are extinguished. Therefore...

It is said: "If one does not look up at Mount Tai, one will not behold its form reaching the thousand-fold heavens; if one does not travel upon the great ocean, one has not seen the marvel of it soaking the sun.
If one does not enter this gate, how can one know its vastness?"

If one does not contemplate the mind, how can one achieve extensive learning? For by understanding that the single faculty of the mind is such that all phenomena are fundamentally natural and universally encompass all scriptures, it is said:
"I only wish to hear little but understand much of the meaning and intent. This is precisely what is meant.
Thus, although the various phenomena are numerous, they are all produced by the single mind; within this one holy path, immeasurable [teachings] are established.
It is like a single fire that receives the names "grass-fire" or "wood-fire" depending on its cause; or like a single water that receives the names "soup" or "wine" according to its function.
From the perspective of its perfect luminosity, it is called a "jewel"; from the perspective of its depth and vastness, it is termed an "ocean";
by virtue of its nature of spiritual understanding, it is designated as the "sacred hall"; and as the source of the myriad dharmas, it is named the "treasury. Thus, it encompasses all.
Every blade of grass is nothing but medicine; every pebble one grasps becomes gold. The entire chamber is filled with nothing but the fragrance of *campaka* flowers;
empty vessels everywhere overflow with the taste of nectar. Lifting one's feet, one never leaves the realm of golden light; turning one's head, everything is a forest of sandalwood.
Thus, the four analytical knowledges and the six supernormal powers arise from this; the three vehicles and the five natures awaken from this.

Therefore, it is said that the Tathāgata never preaches the Dharma, yet he is called one who possesses complete learning (*bahuśruta*). Thus, within the minds of sentient beings, the Buddha does not manifest;
within the mind of the Buddha, sentient beings cannot be apprehended. This may be called the constant turning of the wheel of Dharma, moment after moment within a single mind, without interruption.
If one does not contemplate the mind, how can one practice loving-kindness? Because it would fail to enter into the objectless [samādhi], it would be like a magnet attracting iron;
[only by contemplating the mind] can one spontaneously attract all sentient beings.

If one does not contemplate the mind, how can one exercise compassion? Because one fails to realize that all things share the same essence, everything becomes mere attachment and deluded views. Thus it is said:
"To see my own son as a man and another's child as a woman is to labor in vain with compassionate thoughts born of false imagination."
If one does not contemplate the mind, how can one be born in the Pure Land? Therefore it is said: "All Buddhas of the three periods of time are non-existent;
they exist solely in dependence upon one's own mind. If a Bodhisattva can thoroughly understand that all Buddhas and all phenomena are merely the measure of the mind, [they will attain liberation].

This is identical to the patience of conformity (*anulomikī-kṣānti*). One may enter the first stage (*prathamā bhūmi*), cast off the body, and be swiftly reborn in the world of Abhirati, or be born within the pure Buddha-land of Sukhāvatī.
It is further said: "When wisdom practices the mastery of consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātratā*), one thus attains a pure land.
Thus we know what the ancients said: "The myriad things and myriad forms are all accomplished by the mind. Because the mind has elevations and depressions, hills and mounds arise. This is indeed so.
As for the statement, "The Buddha-land is eternally pure; how could it wait for transformation before being adorned? this refers merely to transforming what ordinary people perceive. Thus it is said:
"To contemplate that the nature of the mind is fundamentally pure, like empty space, is the realm of intrinsic purity.
This realm is the cause. To awaken to this mind through contemplative wisdom is called "Buddha. Initial contemplation is termed the cause; the perfection of contemplation is termed the fruit.
If one discusses self-cultivation, it is the mind-king (*citta-rāja*) being untainted. If one discusses transforming others, it is the mental factors (*caitasika*) attaining liberation.

The source of wisdom merely follows along with the shifting of objects. The mind is like fire; phenomena are like its fuel. If one does not restrain the ground of one’s own mind, it will follow only the flow of various dharmas.

These are all cases of losing the root and becoming deluded regarding the source, following the current while chasing after the branches. If one can suddenly clarify the ground of the mind, [the situation changes].
Following only the flow of all phenomena, one directly realizes the source of the mind. One does not seek liberation from the various sense objects, nor is one bound by a single dharma.

This may be called "reaching the root by investigating the branches" and "finding the source by tracing the stream. Thus, there is spontaneous discernment without effort and spontaneous fulfillment without action.
This single mind is revealed, and the myriad dharmas are like reflections in a mirror. Such is the instruction; this is the ultimate point of return.

Just as eight thousand śrāvakas within the assembly of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* saw the nature of the Tathāgata—like the autumn harvest and winter storage where nothing further needs to be done, or like having reached the place of treasure where there is nowhere else to go—it is therefore said: "My Dharma, after a very long time..."
One must speak of the ultimate truth. If one speaks of provisional or inferior teachings, those of initial capacity will give rise to attachment based on the words.

For instance, ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*) dwell in the indeterminate group; their habitual natures are easily defiled, much like white silk. Thus it is said: "Human nature is like a rapid torrent;
if directed east, it flows east; if directed west, it flows west. It is also like the inchworm (*śalabha*), which becomes yellow when it eats yellow.

If one eats what is green, the body becomes green. Just as within the eighth *ālayavijñāna*, the seeds of the ten dharma-realms are all simultaneously present, they arise as active manifestations according to the power of what has been heard through perfuming (*vāsanā*).
If one hears this contemplation of the mind, the seed of the Buddha-realm naturally unfolds.
Furthermore, each and every one of these is a gateway to the unimpeded sovereignty of dependent origination within the true nature (*tathatā*).
All discourse concerns the true virtues according to reality, for such is the nature of the Dharma. This does not refer to transformations, nor to expedient means as antidotes;
rather, every dharma taught possesses its full power, not merely a partial power. It is like ten images of the ten realms of existence cast from gold:
each individual image fully possesses that gold. It is also like ten sons facing their father: each son fully possesses his father. It is simply a matter of following...
Based on names and designations, there appear to be distinctions; yet in the true nature of reality (*tathatā*), the fundamental and the derivative are identical. As a verse says:

"When various forms and minds manifest, they are like the relief patterns on gold or silver; though different names arise for what is within the gold, they are neither prior to nor subsequent to the gold itself."
It is like images of merit embossed on gold or silver, or the forms of dragons and phoenixes; though the front and back are both gold, the names are merely empty distinctions.
Thus, it is said that the *dharmakāya* flows through the five paths and is called "sentient beings. When the awakened mind does not arise, it is named the Buddha of Immovable Wisdom (*acalajñāna*).
What was previously deluded as sentient beings is, although consisting solely of consciousness, subsequently realized as Buddhahood; yet it is not...
Because it issues from the mind, it is said: "The Dharmakāya, which is not existent according to conditions, manifests without being different from phenomena;
sentient beings, who are not non-existent in their quiescence, are established without being different from the Truth. Thus, the verse says: "The Tathāgata’s pure treasury..."
The *ālaya* of the world is like gold and a finger-ring; they are mutually indistinguishable.

Thus one knows that the sun and moon of the past and present possess no different radiance, and that the mountains, rivers, and phenomena of the world abide eternally. Due to the influence of emotional attachments (*qing*), there appear differences; according to wisdom (*zhi*), distinctions are formed.

Yet, while conceptualization is fundamentally empty and non-existent, it is diverse yet not diverse. Emotional attachment does not exist outside of principle (*li*); though there are differences, there is no separation.
This may be called the single path of true mind, which remains unchanging from beginning to end.
If one does not contemplate the mind, how can one protect the True Dharma? Therefore it is said: "A Bodhisattva need not guard all dharmas;
if a Bodhisattva can simply well-guard their own mind, they will be able to accomplish the wondrous Dharma of all Buddhas. It is further said: "Simply [be] correct..."
The mind does not esteem other forms of learning. If one's own mind is upright, the myriad objects all return to it; if one's own mind is deviant, the various sensory realms become obstructed.

Like a diamond jewel placed in the sun that has no fixed form, or like a crystal bead that changes into various colors according to the preceding objects, it is like the Kalpavṛkṣa tree of the heavens that turns according to the will of the gods;
compared to the realms of the human world, it is formed according to the human mind.
Therefore it is said: "The phenomena of the three realms, whether high or low, I declare to be nothing but mind. Thus, all phenomena are mind, and mind is all phenomena.

It is like water appearing in four ways according to different perceptions; the water itself has no fixed characteristic. It is like a single piece of gold cast into the forms of beings in the five destinies; the gold does not possess separate shapes.

Whether one turns away from awakening or accords with the dust of sensory objects, the mind is fundamentally unmoving. Even if one loathes diversity or abandons distinctions, [the mind remains as it is].

The single true suchness (tathatā) is the knowledge that the ten dharma realms, the five aggregates (skandha), and the three types of worlds are, in their ultimate limit, without difference; they are merely the conceptualization of the mind alone.
As a verse says: "There are no earths nor truths, No lands nor emanations, No Buddhas, Pratyekabuddhas, or Śrāvakas— These are merely the conceptualizations of the mind.
The mind pervades all places, And all places are the mind; Because the mind does not..."

Observe well: the nature of the mind is devoid of all marks (*lakṣaṇa*). It is further said: throughout all oceans of directions, [the mind] dwells in dependence upon the mental conceptions of sentient beings.
Entering with such faith, one destroys attachments and becomes tranquil. One does not rejoice in the Buddha, nor does one grieve over Māra.
Like a magician who has no attachment to his illusions, knowing that illusions arise from his own arts, he is like a trained horse that, seeing its reflection, does not [falter].
It is startling, like a shadow emerging from one's own body. Therefore it is said: "There is not the slightest dharma that can grasp another dharma, for there is no functional agency.
Rather, when a dharma arises, the power of dependent origination is so great that two shadows arise within a single essence, which then stand in mutual relation to one another.
That is to say, it is not separate from the various minds and mental factors; by the power of dependent origination, its nature is such that it arises as a matter of course (*dharmatā*).

Because the object is itself the mind, it is difficult to enter; because the mind is itself the object, it is profoundly deep. Thus, a mustard seed can contain Mount Sumeru, and a speck of dust can hold the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).
Within a jar, the sun and moon, or within a single pore, mountains and rivers are naturally and clearly perceived. Therefore, it is said: "Not..."
To emerge from a circular-walled room and yet know the world is what is meant by "knowing how to return to oneself. Thus it is said: "Returning to the root, one attains the essential meaning;

following after illumination, one loses the source. It is like the fact that all Buddhas possess only the single Dharma-body, yet it appears distinct according to the specific responses of sentient beings.
When the mind is distracted, one perceives only blue; when the intention is pure, one beholds only golden light.
It is like the Dragon King who sends down rain of a single flavor, yet each person perceives it differently according to their station. If one’s karma is pure, it transforms into a string of pearls;

if defiled by sin, it appears as swords and blades. This is just as the wood-mother changes color through the influence of filial thought, or as a golden image radiates light from the power of reverent devotion.
Like a mirror reflecting an image, when the form is curved, the shadow is concave; like a valley echoing a sound, when the speech is boisterous, the resonance is harsh.
Thus we know that ascent and descent depend on oneself, and gain and loss arise from the mind. To drink nectar and tread upon clouds and mists is not bestowed by another;
to lie amidst flames and vomit pus and blood is entirely one's own doing. Who else could temper one in the Sword-Trees and Knife-Mountains? [Only the self can cultivate] the Lotus Throne.

Precious trees. What is it that honors them? Therefore it is said: "When one does good, blessings follow; when one walks in evil, calamity pursues. Like an echo responding to a sound, good and evil are like their respective tones.
They are not bestowed by devas, nāgas, or spirits, nor are they created by ancestors or fathers. That which creates them is the mind.
"Accomplishment" refers to the body and speech. Furthermore, as a verse says: "The mind is the root of all phenomena; the mind is sovereign, the mind is the driver.

If one conceives an evil thought within the mind, it immediately issues in speech and action; the suffering of transgression follows of its own accord, like the wheels following the ruts of a carriage. The mind is the root of all phenomena; the mind is sovereign, the mind is the driver.

If one conceives a virtuous thought within the mind, it immediately issues in speech and action; merit and happiness follow of their own accord, like a shadow following the form. Such is this wondrous [teaching].
Gate. Directly pointing to the ground of the mind: it is like a treasure within a bag; if one does not reach in and show it, who can know of its existence? It is like a store of gold within a room;

if one does not encounter a wise person, by what means could it be excavated? If a pearl were hidden inside one’s inner garment, yet one did not meet a close friend to point it out, how could one become wealthy?
It is like the family treasure of a destitute son; without the guidance of the elder, how could it be realized? How could one compete [with others] otherwise?
One is able to inherit and continue [the lineage]. As a verse says: "For example, like a treasure in the dark, it cannot be seen without a lamp;
if the Buddha-dharma is not explained by someone, even the wise cannot comprehend it."
If one does not contemplate the mind, how can one receive, uphold, read, and recite [the teachings]? By breaking through the dust, one brings forth the great thousandfold world-system sutra scrolls;

by looking up at the void, one transcribes immeasurable true expositions. With every thought-moment, one turns the wheel of Dharma—how could there be anything forgotten? Therefore it is said: "The hands do not hold a scroll."

One constantly reads this sutra, yet the mouth remains silent; one recites all the various scriptures, yet the Buddha does not preach the Dharma; the wondrous voice is perpetually opened, yet the mind does not engage in discursive thought;
it universally illumines the dharma-realm. Therefore, if one encounters the lost texts and the definitive meaning, it is like a lion approaching a person.
If one turns one's back on the meaning and pursues only the words, it is like a foolish dog chasing a clod of earth. Therefore it is said: "What I have taught is the principle, not the words;
what you have taught is the verbal expression, not the meaning. Names and designations are like the clod of earth, while ultimate truth is like the person.

The ignorant dog of ignorance chases after names and words as if they were clods of earth, whereas the lion of the Buddha’s omniscient wisdom attains the principle and transcends names. Thus, those who merely pursue names and words [are like the dog].
It is solely because one does not see one's own nature that sprouts of delusion emerge upon objects and discursive thoughts arise within the mind. The water stirs and the pearl becomes obscured;
the clouds fly and the moon is hidden. As a verse says: "A blind dog barks at the reeds; a blind man sings of thieves and tigers."
Because one follows sounds, confusion ensues; it is truly like having eyes that cannot see. Thus, we know one must possess one's own eyes to develop the fundamental mind.
For this reason, the wise strike the ox but do not strike the cart; the foolish grind the brick but do not grind the mirror. How can grinding a brick illuminate objects?
What purpose is served by striking a cart to advance on the road? Striking the cart only brings toil and hardship to the body, merely refining one's false views to no avail.
To practice in this manner is like polishing a brick; it resembles the Round Teaching (Paryaya-yana) only in name, yet results merely in the inferior vehicle of mere emptiness.

To perceive it thus is to fail to realize that the True Suchness (Tathatā) is the Jewel of the Dharma—the inconceivable Dharma-gate of the great majestic power of all Buddhas. It is like the blazing orb of the sun;
how could it be observed by the infants of external paths? This lofty and perfect seat is not for those of the Lesser Vehicle who are stunted and base.
It is impossible for a mosquito to ascend [Mount Sumeru], and difficult for it to carry Mount Sumeru upon its back; how could a *jiaoliao* sparrow swallow the Bohai Sea?
Only a noble son like Samantabhadra or a great being like Mañjuśrī can directly accept and uphold this, thereby attaining sudden perfection without obstruction.
If one does not contemplate the mind, how can one propagate the Dharma? This is because the single mind is the very foundation of what the Tathāgata has taught;
for it is by relying upon this single mind that the Tathāgata attained accomplishment. Thus, the doctrine, the principle, the practice, and the fruit all rely upon this mind.
From the subtle to the manifest, they never depart from it. Were it possible to attain Buddhahood apart from the mind, such a thing could never exist.
Any teaching that exists apart from this [principle of] contemplation belongs to the doctrines of external paths. Therefore, it is said:
"That which is called the Dharma refers to the mind of sentient beings. This mind encompasses all mundane and supramundane dharmas.
Based upon this mind, the meaning of the Mahāyāna is revealed. As a verse states: "If all is but mind alone, where in the world could anything abide? Coming and going..."

Relying on what dharma? How does one see it within the ground [of reality]? Like a bird in the empty sky, moving by means of the wind of the mind, neither dwelling nor observing, yet appearing upon the earth—so too do all these sentient beings, moved by the winds of conceptualization, come and go within their own minds like birds flying through the air.
Seeing the body, the requisites of life, and the vessel-world, the Buddha taught that the mind is thus; therefore, know this.
If one does not recognize the mind, it cannot be called propagating the Dharma. Therefore, it is said: "All dharmas emerge entirely from within the mind;

the mind is itself the Mahāyāna, and the mind is itself Buddha-nature. Furthermore, the mind encompasses all teachings. By observing the minds of all sentient beings, one finds that they are fully endowed with all dharma-gates.
The Tathāgata clearly and thoroughly examines their mental phenomena and, according to those minds, expounds immeasurable teachings.
They emerge from the mind; although their names and meanings are inexhaustible, they equally elucidate the one mind.

Therefore, it is said that in the *Avataṃsaka* and other sutras, the negation of external objects and the affirmation of consciousness-only is termed "mind-only" (*cittamātra*). In the *Madhyāntavibhāga*, the negation of the paths of extremist attachment is termed the "Middle Way."

In the *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtras*, that which clarifies the nature of discernment (*pravicaya*) is called "prajñā. In the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, that which clarifies the ultimate intent of transport is termed the "One Vehicle" (*ekayāna*).
In the *Śrīmālādevī Siṃhanāda Sūtra*, that which excludes other false constructs is termed the "Truth of the Single Reality" (*eka-tattva-satya*);

as it reveals the root of all phenomena, it is also termed the "Single Reliance" (*eka-śaraṇa*). Realized through emptiness, it is also termed "emptiness" (*śūnyatā*). These [terms] manifest distinct differences.
Emerging from the entanglements, it reveals and encompasses the Buddha’s virtues. Because the Buddha emerges from within this, it is called the *tathāgatagarbha*.

Its essence being unstained, its true *dharmatā* is called the intrinsically pure mind (*prakṛti-prabhāsvara-citta*). As the very substance of its meritorious qualities, it is also called the *dharmakāya*. (From the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-sūtra*)

The principle of negation is without differentiation; this is called the Dharma-gate of Non-duality. In the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, it is expressed as being without arising or ceasing, and is also termed "neither born nor extinguished.
In the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, it reveals the cause of the Dharmakāya and is frequently termed "Buddha-nature," characterized by liberation from bondage.
It is also called *nirvāṇa*. In the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*, it is designated as "inconceivable" (*acintya*) to indicate its transcendence of verbal expression.

In the *Yogācārabhūmi* and other texts, it is designated as "non-established" (*apratiṣṭhita*) to reveal that it cannot be conceptually constructed. In the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* and other treatises, it is designated as "perfected reality" (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*) to manifest its universality, permanence, and so forth.
In the *Abhidharmakośa* and other works, it is termed "suchness" (*tathatā*) to clarify that it is not false or inverted. Thus, all phenomena follow the mind.
Thus they abide. Their praise is inexhaustible; they simply accord with the one mind, which inherently contains all virtues. Therefore it is said:
"The Ultimate Sage bestowed his teachings to mirror the profound pinnacle of the one mind; the Great Being propagated and expounded them to illuminate the subtle essence of these cryptic words.

Although he has forgotten his concerns within the realm of interpretation, he traverses the vast ocean of literary meaning. This is because he desires to entrust the traces of the phenomenal world to the symbols of the written word, in order to exhaustively [realize the truth]."
It is an inexhaustible realm. Thus we know that without words, one cannot establish its literary expression; without literary expression, one cannot broaden its meaning;
and without meaning, one cannot fathom its profundity. Now, he who attains this profundity realizes the principle of the inexhaustible single mind.
Therefore, a verse says: "If one wishes to teach and transform all sentient beings throughout the trichiliocosm, as..."

The clouds spread widely, reaching everywhere; according to their faculties and desires, all are made to rejoice. The assemblies of Buddhas at the tip of a single hair are beyond numbering, and the mental inclinations of sentient beings are likewise infinite.
To each, one provides a dharma-gate in accordance with their mind; throughout the entire dharma-realm, it is thus.

If the Dharma is propagated on such a vast scale, how could its benefit ever be exhausted? Directly pointing to one's own mind, the family treasure is fully presented, like emptying out the contents of a bag.
Invertedly stored, it is a great, unobstructed giving that penetrates both fruit and cause, leaving nothing before or after;
it may be called the limit of benefit within a single thought-moment and a single instant. Thus it is said:

"The realm of Vairocana, the mysterious gate of all wonders—where the wisdom-knowledge speaks of it without end, where Sudhana draws from it without exhaustion, where Mañjuśrī embodies it in profound stillness, and where Samantabhadra realizes it."

This is done through the successive layers [of manifestation]. Therefore, if one follows its *dharmatā* (dharma-nature), it is like clouds dispersing across the vast sky—originally there is not a single thing.
If one follows its function of wisdom (*jñāna-prayoga*), it is like flowers blooming in a spring valley—the Buddha-activities are all-pervasive.

Although they are said to pervade as many worlds as there are grains of sand in the Ganges, they all equally conform to the One Way. Thus it is said: "Within a single word or phrase, the Tathāgata expounds an ocean of boundless sūtras."

If one does not contemplate the mind, how can one establish the *bodhimaṇḍa*? Because knowing all phenomena in a single thought is the accomplishment of the *bodhimaṇḍa*, for it is the realization of all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*).
Furthermore, it is said that all sentient beings are the *bodhimaṇḍa*, because they possess the characteristic of immovability. Moreover, as for the *bodhimaṇḍa*:

the principle of the true reality (*bhūtatathatā*) pervading everywhere is the "field" (*maṇḍa*), and the universal realization through the myriad practices is the "path" (*mārga*). Thus, the path is non-...

There is nowhere he does not reach; there is no place where he is not present. If one can harbor the *dōjō* within the breast and cast away myriad burdens beyond the body, then even though the form remains amidst the clamor and the traces are adjacent to worldly affairs, wherever one travels amidst movement, it is nothing other than the *dōjō*.
For this reason, the Bodhisattva Qizhige (Abandoning All Coverings) addressed the Buddha, saying: “World-Honored One, I have heard that the Tathāgata sits at the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*).
Where does this path lie? Is it near or far? Can it be seen? The Buddha said: “Good son, the Dharma-body is all-pervasive;

there is nowhere that is not a Buddha-field. Throughout the worlds of the ten directions, within the monasteries of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), their nature is empty and self-detached—this is precisely the Path.”

[The Buddha said: "What do you mean by asking whether it is near or far? Good son, if one can awaken to and understand that the Way resides within body and mind, such a person is said to have 'seen all dharmas.
Furthermore, it is said: 'When I sat at the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa), I did not obtain a single dharma;
I obtained only the ultimate emptiness arising from inverted afflictions. It was obtained through non-attainment.'"
One knows by virtue of having nothing to know.

If one does not contemplate the mind, how can one clarify the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*)? All phenomena, whether conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) or unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), arise from the mind;
there is nothing that is not the mind. Because the mind does not abide in its own nature, it can follow the conditions of defilement or purity to manifest the ten [realms].

The characteristic of the dharma-realm is therefore called "dharma-characteristic" (dharmalakṣaṇa). Because it does not lose its own nature even while correctly following conditions, it is called "dharma-nature" (dharmatā).

Thus, following conditions while lacking inherent nature, and lacking inherent nature while following conditions, is like water that does not maintain its own nature but forms waves according to the wind.
When waves are actually forming, they do not lose their moist nature; if they were to lose their moist nature, they could not become waves. The nature of the mind is likewise.

Thus, one knows that both the dharmatā (the nature of phenomena) and the dharmalakṣaṇa (the characteristics of phenomena), as well as the gates of the ultimate and conventional meanings, are all established by the pure true mind of the Tathāgatagarbha.
Whether good or evil, they revolve according to the mind; if they revolve in accordance [with reality], they are termed nirvāṇa. Therefore...
It is said: "The mind creates all Tathāgatas; if one proceeds in reverse, this is birth and death. Therefore it is said: "The three realms are empty and illusory, all produced by the single mind.
It is like the substance of water, which has neither square nor round form; when it enters a square vessel, it becomes square, and when it enters a round vessel, it becomes round.
Therefore it is said: "The Buddhas are neither devas nor humans, yet they can manifest as devas and humans; appearing as devas when among devas, and appearing as humans when among humans.
As a verse says: "Just as the power of a single mind can give rise to various minds, so too does the body of one Buddha universally manifest as all Buddhas.
To penetrate this way is to realize that the single realm is without differentiation—neither past nor present, neither increasing nor decreasing.
There is no decrease. As a verse says: "Suppose a person digs up earth from a road and fashions it into an image.
A fool says the image has come into being, while the wise say it is merely road-earth. Later, when he wishes to travel on the road, he takes the image back and fills the road with it.
The image was never subject to arising or ceasing, nor is the road newly made or old. Thus, arising and ceasing differ according to conditions, while newness and antiquity differ according to time.

Investigating it from beginning to end, there is but one path of earth; moreover, while the sages of past and present differ in their states of delusion and enlightenment, when viewed from first to last, they are but the single consciousness of the mind.
Thus, one perceives the vast height and breadth of one's own mind, which illuminates the infinite responses of the sages.

Consequently, those who have not yet understood are led to understanding, and those who have not yet found peace are enabled to find peace. Its grace covers the great trichiliocosm, and its compassion encompasses the entire dharma-realm. Therefore:

It is said: "One should study the Prajñāpāramitā so as to provide illumination for the world of darkness and for every interval between worlds where the light of the sun, moon, and other luminaries does not reach. This is what that means.

If one does not contemplate the mind, how can there be adornment? The *dharmakāya* of all Buddhas is like the appearance of pure gold; the marks and signs (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*) are like gold fashioned into ornaments.

Just as the substance and function of gold are entirely identical when it is made into an ornament, so too do form and nature manifest from the mind, with no duality between their essence and characteristics.
As it is asked: "If the Buddha’s *dharmakāya* possesses no various differentiated forms and signs, how can it manifest such variety?"
Regarding all forms: the answer is that because the *dharmakāya* is the substantial reality of form, it is able to manifest various kinds of forms.
That is to say, from the very beginning, form and mind are non-dual. The original nature of the color of sand is the self-nature of the mind; this is called the *jñānakāya*.
Because the original nature of the mind is the self-nature of form, it is called the *dharmakāya*. Based upon the *dharmakāya*, all Tathāgatas manifest their *rūpakāyas*.
Pervading all places without interruption, and because all boundless Buddha-activities arise from a single mind;
because of the canopies of all jewels produced from the *pāramitās*; because of the flower curtains produced from the pure understanding of all Buddha-realms;
because of the garments produced from the realization of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*); [they] enter the adamantine Dharma...
Because all nets of bells produced by the obstructing mind are resolved as being like illusions, and all solid fragrances and so forth are produced by the mind,
the bodhisattva does not depend on external adornments to accomplish all phenomena, for they are inherently complete within a single mind.
Therefore, all sensory objects are the mind, and they all fulfill the work of Buddhahood. Thus it is said: "The jeweled nets upon the cloud-platforms all proclaim wondrous sounds;
the light from every pore is able to preach the Dharma. In the world of Gandhavatī, the samādhi is manifested by eating fragrant food;

in the Buddha-land of Sukhāvatī, right mindfulness is perfected by listening to the wind through the trees. Stringed and wind instruments can transmit the mind, and one may perceive it through direct observation.
To preserve the Way: since both speech and silence, as well as seeing and blinking, are all forms of teaching, then seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing are all means of listening.

If one can attain the Dharma and harmonize with the spirit, why must it necessarily depend on verbal expression? It is like a physiognomist who divines a person’s character by observing their facial complexion to discern the signs of nobility or commonality.
The sound of non-Buddhists striking skulls allows them to discern matters of good and evil; Aśvaghoṣa possessed the skill of the *vīṇā*;
Śakra had ministers of Dharma-music. Through the lute, one’s intent was conveyed to the King of Qin, saving him from the hands of Jing Ke;
Sima Xiangru harmonized with Lady Wenjun, ultimately gaining her to follow his carriage. Thus we know that whether it be form or sound, all are fully contained within the Dharma of the One Mind.
Therefore it is said: "All forms are the Buddha’s forms; all sounds are the Buddha’s sounds.
If one does not contemplate the mind, how can one realize Bodhi? For Bodhi is the Way, and the Way is the self-nature pure mind—tranquil and unmoving.
This is precisely the true wisdom of unconditioned perfect enlightenment; its Way is void and profound.
It is wondrously beyond the ordinary realm. Listeners have no means to contain its hearing; the wise have no means to employ their knowledge; the eloquent have no means to apply their speech;
and those who depict it have no means to describe its form. Thus it is said: "The bodhicitta is neither existent nor created;
it is free from words and letters. Bodhi is itself the mind, and the mind is itself sentient beings. If one can understand it thus...
Explanation: This is called the Bodhisattva’s cultivation of the bodhicitta. Because one realizes this mind, one attains enlightenment; therefore, it is termed "ultimate.
There is not a single thought that does not become universal illumination, for a single thought is instantaneously perfected.

There is not a single dharma that is not permeated by light, for there is no dharma outside of thought. As it is said: "There is no suchness outside of wisdom, for it is that which is entered by wisdom."
Furthermore, there is no wisdom external to suchness that can realize suchness. It is also said: "There is not even the slightest dharma that coexists with dharmas.
Thus we know this is the Dharma-gate of the single limit of Mind-only; outside the mind, there is no further dharma that can be held in opposition or that can coexist.
Therefore it is said: "The mind does not reach the object; the object does not reach the mind. Whatever object is perceived is merely the mind being perceived.
Thus, on the ground of ultimate reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), neither the Buddhas can traverse nor reach it, nor can the Great Māra traverse or reach it.
This is because both Buddhas and Māras are equally the single mind of ultimate reality (*bhūtakoṭi*). If one were able to traverse or reach it, they would become two separate dharmas.
Why is this? If there were a person capable of practicing and reaching [enlightenment], then there would be dharmas that are practiced and reached.

To have dharmas external to the mind does not constitute bodhi. Now, however, whether contrary or compliant, all things return to the same source; whether beautiful or evil, they share the same essence. There is nothing that is not bodhi.
As it is said, "The five heinous crimes are themselves bodhi. Since the five heinous crimes and bodhi do not transcend the nature of the mind, they are one.
Therefore, the celestial Māra is the Dharma-realm; birth-and-death is itself the gate of Nirvāṇa. When discussing the true reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*), one does not destroy conventional designations;
when analyzing distinctions, one does not undermine equality. The eyes do not see impure lands; the ears do not hear loathsome sounds.
Even the sūtras of the non-Buddhist Nirgranthas are all the Buddha’s teachings. Thus spoke Devadatta.

Regarding the discourse: when all [teachings] accord with the true principle, then thorns cast the shade of seven layers of rows of trees, and even crows and manticores preach the profound meaning of the One Path.
Thus it is said: "Like a vessel of lapis lazuli, wherever it may be placed, it does not lose its nature.
Know that the mind is likewise: defiled dharmas flow along with it without increasing, and pure dharmas flow back against them without decreasing. If...

If it is manifested through emptiness, it appears as emptiness; if it is manifested through form, it appears as form. Following the conditions of the dharma-realm, it manifests throughout the entire dharma-realm.
Its manifestation is devoid of the nature of manifestation; as condition follows upon condition, they are themselves empty.

There is only the single true mind, profound and unmoving. As a verse says: "The Buddhas attain liberation from the mind; the mind is stainless and called pure. The five paths are fresh and clean, not..."

One is defiled by sensations. Those who understand this achieve the Great Way; thus, the five paths arise from the mind. Although it pervades the cinnabar terrace, it remains untainted and eternally pure.

It expands to encompass the six realms without becoming vast, and contracts to fit within a single speck of dust without overflowing. Even when wearing fur or bearing horns, its fundamental nature does not differ;
even when the soul disperses and the form dissolves, this single spirit remains forever present.

If one does not contemplate the mind, how can one be complete in the factors of the path? Since body, sensation, mind, and phenomena are but the single true mind, and all lack self-nature and are ultimately ungraspable—this is the contemplation of the four foundations of mindfulness.
That wholesome and unwholesome dharmas are transformed and produced from the mind is the four right efforts.
That the nature of the mind is empty and pervasive, manifesting and concealing with sovereign ease, is the four bases of psychic power. That the mind of faith is firm and profound...
If it is like empty space, that is the five faculties and the five powers. If the awakening mind does not arise, that is the seven factors of enlightenment.

To directly realize the nature of the mind as being neither deviant nor correct is the eightfold noble path. When the mind and its objects are harmoniously integrated such that self and others are of one essence, that is the four means of integration.
If one’s body, speech, and mind do not constantly follow the practice of wisdom, this is precisely the eighteen unique qualities (*āveṇika-dharma*).

From the perfection of the causes of the myriad practices through the fulfillment of the fruits of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*), up until receiving the prediction (*vyākaraṇa*) of Buddhahood, all of this is never apart from the single mind. Therefore it is said:
"When the mind is pure and free from defilement, one receives the prediction. It is also said: "Without grasping at a single dharma, the Buddhas swiftly bestow the prediction. This...
The Gate of the Single Mind: The nature of spirit stands independently; it has never been identical with any single dharma, nor has it ever been separate from any single dharma;

it has never been the same as any single dharma, nor has it ever been different from any single dharma. Why is this? Because there are no dharmas outside the mind, and seeing dharmas is seeing the mind;

therefore, it is called the gate of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), the wondrousness that transcends all dependencies. It is like when Mañjuśrī treads upon a place, the entire ground becomes gold, or when Sāgara-mati arrives...
It is purely water. Therefore it is said: "All dharmas are the measure of the one mind; there are no dharmas outside the mind.
Since there are no dharmas outside the mind, how could one dharma of the mind create an obstacle for another dharma of the mind?
Nor could one dharma of the mind bring about liberation for another dharma of the mind. There is neither obstacle nor liberation. It is further said: "One does not perceive even a single..."

The severance of all dharmas is the characteristic of bodhi. Without realizing a single dharma, one realizes all dharmas; therefore, it is called the Perfectly Complete Enlightenment (Samyaksaṃbodhi).
These six sovereign kings are eternally pure: when they are ordinary beings, they are ordinary beings; when they are sages, they are sages.

The great waters do not confine; how could delusion and awakening be fixed? The fundamental causes of the faculties of sentient beings and the very life-nature of all Buddhas simply arise according to conditions and do not compete with external things.
Like a south-pointing chariot, all things return to the same destination; like a *kengxi* (a hairpin that keeps chickens from scratching), it remains upright in every direction.
Therefore it is said: To be able to know that all things are but this single mind is called "mastery over the mind.
Then the inexhaustible treasures of the Dharma-wealth will constantly emerge from the palm of one's hand, and all the empty spaces of the ten directions will become treasuries of wisdom.

If one does not believe in one's own Dharma but instead grasps at external objects, it is like reaching up to pluck a distant star, casting oneself into the water to catch the moon’s reflection, or blowing upon a fishing net.
If one wishes to fill the air with fragrance, yet takes only its scent to place inside a basket, how could it ever be obtained? It is utterly futile.
Now, to grasp at superior and wondrous objects is like a beautiful woman who loves her own reflection in a mirror;

to loathe and turn away from adverse conditions is like a wild horse that fears its own shadow in the midday sun. Furthermore, to grasp at objects is like seeking emptiness within emptiness; to abandon the Dharma...

People, if they fear emptiness and run about wildly, grasping and rejecting while not departing from within emptiness, and harboring both hatred and love within their minds, will, through improper contemplation, produce these inverted views.
As a verse says: "The dharmas spoken through words and phrases Are falsely discriminated by those of small wisdom;
Therefore, obstacles arise. They do not understand their own mind. If one cannot understand one's own mind, How can there be wisdom?"
The Right Path. Through perverted perceptions, one increases all evils. It is further said: "The ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya) is nothing but mind alone.
If one does not understand the mind, everything becomes conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya). Therefore it is said: "Viewed with the fleshly eye, there is nothing true that is not mundane;
viewed with the Dharma-eye, there is nothing mundane that is not true. However, if one realizes the mind, then the fleshly eye is itself the Buddha-eye.

If one does not understand the mind, then the divine eye becomes a cataract-affected eye. As it is said, "The Great Being’s physical eye is the perfect penetration, whereas the divine eyes of the Two Vehicles possess cataracts.
Furthermore, since the Two Vehicles attain the divine eye through the cultivation of untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*), how could it instead become an obscuring cataract?

This is because, although the two teachings of the *Zang* (Treatise) and *Tong* (Shared) vehicles possess the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍ-abhijñā*), they cannot, within a single moment of mind, fully embody the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*). All of them...

The cessation of the mind constitutes the ultimate fruit. Even if one follows the distinct teachings of the Mahāyāna and is able to know that all dharmas tend toward [the truth], this mind has not yet attained full perfection;
it must undergo distinct stages of cultivation, arising sequentially, remaining within the path of gradual teaching rather than entering the path of perfect penetration.
This gate of contemplation is received directly only by those of the highest faculties.
If one does not contemplate the mind, how can the work of Buddhahood be accomplished? Since the myriad dharmas revolve according to the mind, they skillfully bring all things to completion.

This enables the ordinary and the sagely to penetrate one another, the great and the small to contain one another, the hidden and the manifest to mutually complete one another, and the one and the many to be harmoniously integrated. Therefore it is said: "Contemplate..."
The King of the Emptiness of Mind is profound and subtle, difficult to fathom; it is formless and signless, yet possesses great spiritual power. Therefore it is said:
"These offering implements are all sealed by the dharma of non-action and accomplished by the unsurpassed mind. Thus, the mountains and rivers of the Flower Treasury World...
All accomplish the work of Buddhahood; this is what Sudhana perceives and sees as they all enter the Dharma-gates.

When a Wheel-Turning King sits upon his wondrous jeweled throne, he enters the four *dhyānas* and remains detached from the five desires. When a Bodhisattva dons the crown of the *dharmatā*, he perceives all phenomena as manifest within his own mind.
At times, he is silent and still, revealing the wondrous through the wheel of the mind; at other times, amidst the signlessness of empty space, he transforms King Aśoka.
Through awakening to the truth, the *kāṣāya* robe is suspended from a lofty banner and fragrant food is taken from the highest realms. Sometimes the Way is preserved through direct perception;
sometimes the mind is transmitted through extraordinary signs. Thus, even a single hair’s breadth of the light of wisdom-mind manifests the various Buddha-activities within the realm of worldly toil.
This extends even to the accumulation of the mountains and rivers of the Great Iron Ring Mountains within the body of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, or within the womb of Māyā.
Within [a single atom], they unfold unspeakable worlds; within a single mote of dust, they behold inconceivable Buddha-lands.

Upon the tip of a needle, they establish infinite clouds of bodies; they condense the vast expanse of the four oceans into a single pore, and contain the towering height and breadth of Mount Sumeru within a mustard seed.
They fly Buddha-fields throughout the ten directions without shifting their original locations, and cast the great trichiliocosm into...
Beyond the realms, sentient beings remain unaware: the sun and moon hang from the tip of a hair, and offerings appear within the body.
The belly contains the flames that consume the kalpa, yet the fire burns as if it were ordinary; the mouth inhales the winds of the ten directions, yet the body suffers no diminution.
All of this is the transformation of one's own mind: without moving, distance and proximity are suddenly distinguished; in a single thought, all is encompassed—unimpeded, whether large or small.
They interpenetrate one another. Some say that the Land of Fragrant Accumulation is forty-two Ganges-sands of worlds away from here;

this refers to traversing the forty-two stages of the Dharma-gate of the Mind-Ground. Others say that when flowers and necklaces were scattered, they formed a jeweled terrace with four pillars in mid-air;
this is the Nirvana of the four virtues of the One Mind: permanence, bliss, self, and purity. Therefore it is said:
These flower canopies and so forth are all produced from the *anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti* (the patient endurance of the non-arising of phenomena). Alternatively, the Buddha said:
"The king of deer at that time was none other than myself. Thus, he connects the past and the present to clarify the dharma of the single limit of one's own mind.

Furthermore, whenever there is a voice issuing from the sky within the teachings to provide instruction and cause doubts to subside upon hearing it, these are all instances of the sudden awakening to one's own mind.
It is not the realm of others. For example, when Master Jietuo (Vimokṣa) encountered a transformation Buddha, he inquired about the profound meaning.
The Buddha then concealed his body and did not appear, but spoke a verse from mid-air, saying: "Skillful means and wisdom serve as a lamp; they illuminate the realm of the mind.
If you wish to know the true Dharma, there is nothing whatsoever to be seen. By this, he awakened to the Way. Furthermore, King Laṅkā heard the Buddha...
After the preaching of the Dharma, the Buddha and the fourfold assembly suddenly vanished. Reflecting upon this, he immediately entered into the principle of "Mind-Only.
Alternatively, when the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* transports devas and humans to other lands, this is precisely the threefold transformation of the field of the mind.
Or, when Vimalakīrti brings the goddess Māyādevī to this region, this is the manifestation of purity within the defiled. Or, when a room of one zhang accommodates a high seat and a jeweled canopy—

Manifesting throughout the great trichiliocosm, he has not yet departed from Tuṣita, yet he has already entered parinirvāṇa; without rising from beneath the king of trees, he ascends to the Trāyastriṃśa heaven.

Holding hands for immeasurable kalpas, he ascends the pavilion to behold the causes of the three periods of time. From the space between Śākyamuni’s eyebrows emerges the manifestation of clouds of bodhisattva bodies;
from the pores of Samantabhadra are shown the gateways to the realms of all Buddhas. From a small vessel emerges the infinite...
Exquisite delicacies are limited, yet rare treasures rain from the void beyond measure; without moving from this place, they pervade the entire site of enlightenment.
Ten *kṣetra* jewel-monasteries merge into a single land. Hearing the sutra for fifty minor eons is like the duration of a single *kṣaṇa*;
manifesting supernatural powers for seven days extends them to a great eon, just as Wang Qi encountered the immortals.
A single game of chess may take three years, yet it is perceived as a mere moment of eating; King Mu of Zhou followed the illusory man for many years, yet he felt it was but an instant.
Thus, one can perceive the short as long and the long as short. Therefore, we know that it is not a matter of the duration of kalpas, but is merely formed by consciousness alone.
Even the meanings of the six characteristics and the ten mysterious gates are all the perfect fusion of the One Mind.

They manifest without obstruction. Regarding the meaning of the six aspects: first, a single mind is the general characteristic (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*), while manifold minds are the particular characteristics (*viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa*).

This extends to their being identical or different, and their being established or destroyed—all are the provisional constructions of the beginning and end of the single mind. As for the ten mysteries (*daśa-guhya-mukha*):
The gate of simultaneous and perfect correspondence; the gate of the mutual inclusion of the one and the many without confusion;

and so on, up to the gates of concealment and manifestation, the Indra’s net, the possession of virtues, sovereign mastery, formal establishment, the ten periods of time, and the reliance upon phenomena—all of these are skillfully perfected as a single gate through the turning of the mind.
Thus, immeasurable teachings and meanings are simultaneously accomplished by means of the mind of equality.
This is the meaning of identity. That the differentiated minds are many is the meaning of multiplicity. That one mind is all minds is the meaning of mutual identity (*xiāngjí*).
This is the meaning of simultaneous correspondence (*tóngshí xiāngyìng*). That all minds enter into one mind is the meaning of mutual inclusion (*xiāngrù*).
That one mind encompasses all minds is the meaning of concealment (*yǐnyì*). That all minds support one mind is the meaning of manifestation (*xiǎnyì*). Because they are not destroyed...

To manifest a mind of equality while possessing a mind of differentiation is the meaning of "the one within the many. To manifest a mind of differentiation while not concealing a mind of equality is the meaning of "the many within the one.
Furthermore, the subtle mind does not obstruct the vast mind, and the vast mind does not obstruct the subtle mind;
this is the meaning of the non-identity of the one and the many. Because the single true mind is pure, it is differentiated.
The mind is both manifold and differentiated, yet this differentiated mind is itself the one true mind; thus, the manifold is eternally the pure. The one true mind is itself the differentiated mind;

thus, the pure is eternally the manifold. This is the principle of the mutual purity and mixture of all the *ālayas*: by means of the one mind encompassing all minds, they in turn enter back into the one mind.
This is the meaning of the Indra’s Net. The manifestation of objects from the mind and the consciousness of that mind is the meaning of "relying on phenomena to reveal the Dharma.

Long kalpas and short kalpas—the extension and contraction of temporal measures—are all formed through the accumulation of thoughts; they are manifested by the single mind. This is the meaning of the ten periods of time.

Based on the correct principle of the single mind, inconceivable Dharma-gates are expounded. Their ultimate point of return transcends words and is beyond thought; it is simply the turning back of the mind-only.
Regarding the meaning of transformation: since one’s own mind is thus, the minds of others are likewise so. Pure entry into the interlacing net is layered and inexhaustible;

all are points of entry for those with perfect capacity, each capable of receiving one’s steps and providing a place to settle the spirit. For instance, even through observing flavors or smelling fragrances, one can all realize the Way.

Flowers fall and bracelets jingle; all these may serve as evidence of the Real. Speech and silence are always in accord; the profound and subtle, whether in motion or stillness, never depart from the Dharma-realm.

Even the vast collection of meanings, numbering as many as the sands of the Ganges, and the infinite gates of Dharma—taking one example to illustrate the rest—they all do not transcend the phenomena of one’s own mind.
Therefore, we know that whatever a Bodhisattva performs in accordance with the world all manifests the mind. As the Vimalakīrti Sūtra says: "Without abandoning the Path..."

The Dharma manifests the affairs of ordinary beings; as it is said, "In a single thought-moment, in all places, for the sake of all sentient beings, one manifests the attainment of perfect enlightenment.
This is the garden of the Bodhisattva, for the *dharmakāya* pervades all worlds throughout the entirety of space.

Thus, one knows that there is no need to employ the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*) to see through to the limits of the ten directions—what need is there for the divine eye? To hear the Dharma everywhere, one does not rely on the divine ear (*divyaśrotra*).

Regarding the sound of the elements: how could it depend on [external] instruments? With the supernormal power of the divine feet, one reaches the lands of the ten directions with speed, yet remains seated upright and motionless;
the Buddhas are constantly manifest before one. As for the lute of the *kiṃnara*, how could its resonance require the adjustment of strings and frets?
